title: How (and Why) to Ask Administrators for PD Funding
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart begins with the claim that US schools spend billions on professional development much of which is wasted, citing TNTP's Dan Weisberg, and argues that one remedy is teachers owning their own growth. He identifies the feelings that stop teachers asking for funding, namely being overwhelmed, scared, guilty and, for some women, reluctant to negotiate, and answers each in turn. His central stance is that teachers are professionals like doctors and lawyers who need ongoing training, and that PD money is earmarked for exactly this purpose. The second half is a practical script: pick one skill need within half an hour, find an expert resource, gather the facts on time and cost, craft the argument, request a short meeting and state the ask directly. He ends with the advice not to back-pedal after the ask but to wait for the answer.
points: Stuart pairs the TNTP finding that PD dollars are largely wasted with the argument that the most powerful development is chosen by teachers themselves.
He dismantles four internal barriers to asking (survival mode, fear, guilt and a gender gap in negotiating) and says most principals would welcome such requests.
The professional-versus-technician framing, comparing teachers to doctors and lawyers, justifies treating ongoing training as a normal investment rather than a favour.
The how-to is concrete: diagnose one urgent skill need in under half an hour, pick an expert resource, document time and cost, and make the case in a short meeting.
He supplies a fill-in-the-blank script and the warning to resist softening the ask, which turns a vague intention into a rehearsed professional move.
quotes: Unfortunately, much of this money is wasted. As Dan Weisberg of TNTP puts it, “We are bombarding teachers with a lot of help, but the truth is, it’s not helping all that much. We are not approaching this in a very smart way. We’re basically throwing a lot of things against the wall and not even looking to see whether it works.

The most powerful professional development of my career has almost always been selected for me, by me. It’s been attending local workshops with experts, or going to conferences, or reading books and studies in search of answers to my burning questions, or taking online courses from thinkers I respect. It’s the professional development I’ve received after standing back and asking, “What am I wrestling with? Why does it matter? Who might be able to help?

Survival Mode is antithetical to Flourishing Mode. If we want to flourish, we have to at some point carve out 20 or 40 or 60 minutes from the whirlwind and ask ourselves, “What would really help?” This’ll cost you an hour today and save you the next 180+ days on the job.

Many principals I’ve met are dying to have the “problem” of a teacher walking into their office and saying, “Hey, let me tell you how you can help me be awesome at my job.” If yours isn’t like that, it’s likely that inside of them there is that person who wants to be the kind of principal the delights in teachers owning their own development, but toxic stress has locked that person up behind a wall.

At the end of the day, it comes down to this: we’re professionals, not technicians. We’re like doctors and lawyers. Don’t tell me what society says — I don’t even know who “society” is. Ours is complex and professional and socially critical work. That means we need ongoing training to stay competent. Let’s act like it.

Second, find an expert who is offering professional development about that skill. It can be a book, or a course, or a conference, or some other newfangled thing. But find something that could help you move the work forward quickly in real life.

I’ve found in myself that right after a big ask, there’s a temptation to back pedal, to soften: “Of course, I might be able to just get by….” or “It’s probably too much money…” DON’T DO THIS. Just state your case, ask if you can sign up, and wait.
